## Constraints for later execution

- M01/M02 verifiers hard-code 15 pages and 16 destinations, plus artwork page positions. New teaching pages need explicit builder changes and corresponding justified checks.
- All chapter source parsers expect recognised worked-decision/check/answer/reminder blocks. Additional independent checks need a deliberate parser/verification extension.
- M03–M10 support continuation pages; oversized indivisible panels still hit the shared overflow guard. M09 does not currently render Markdown tables as tables, so its proposed pollutant/powertrain tables need an approved presentation and builder handling.
- Chapter references are batched four per page. New aliases can add reference pages. Existing source-check dates are historical, not verification of new claims.
- Sign placements use exact manuscript quotes; preserve anchors or revise placement records and validate artwork.
- Existing navigation records have at least two local pages between each recorded question and its answer. This is a read-only metadata check, not fresh visual verification. Preserve spacing and recheck global page parity after assembly.
- Assembly verification hard-codes 498 pages, labels, map size and footer boundary. Update all affected checks during G11 without weakening text/link fidelity checks.
- The coverage generator stores reviewed decisions and page numbers in code; an unchanged rerun cannot independently assess added teaching. G12 must use freshly reviewed evidence.

# G1 completed — Chapter 1

Completed 12 October 2026. All four assigned questions have adequate teaching and verified official evidence in the standalone chapter. Five essential claims checked; no answer conflicts or blockers.

| Question | Teaching | Check | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| situation-062: stimulant overconfidence / masked fatigue | 5 | 6 | 13 |
| situation-068: microsleep | 5 | 6 | 13 |
| situation-069: adequate sleep | 5 | 6 | 13 |
| situation-129: Vision Zero | 1, 7 | 8 | 13 |

These are **local Chapter 1 pages**, not final book pages.

Chapter 1 grows from 15 to 17 pages: one text teaching page, one additional reference page. The existing four lessons, chapter identifier, artwork and page design remain. No new design was required.

Trafikverket provides Vision Zero's aim and shared-responsibility explanation directly. Inspected TS/TRV pages did not supply sufficient precise physiological detail for the other claims. Documented official fallbacks: CDC/NIOSH for microsleep, NHTSA for sleep and reduced perceived fatigue, and a Swedish Government proposition published by Riksdagen for stimulant confidence/judgement. Historical pharmacology passages are used only with qualified wording; no historical or foreign driving laws are imported. See [evidence](evidence.md) for versions, locators and applicability limits.

Original teaching explains each principle, gives a practical example, and supplies comprehension checks with reasoning on the separated answer page. The distance calculation is explicitly hypothetical: 90 km/h ÷ 3.6 × 2 seconds = 50 metres.

Validation: complete manuscript fidelity, citation URLs, internal navigation, embedded fonts, text bounds, original approved asset hashes, assessment separation, reproducible build and delivery checksum all pass. All 17 rendered pages inspected; detailed checks on new/changed teaching, assessment, answers and references. See [validation](validation.json) and [question coverage](coverage.json).

The question bank, both 498-page review PDFs, baseline audit and G0 snapshots remain unchanged. M02–M10 teaching text is unchanged. G1 is complete at chapter level; G11 will assemble the revised book and assign final pages, followed by G12's whole-bank audit. G2 has not been executed.

questions.teaching_excerpt: Stimulation is not safe judgement. Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement · NHTSA: stimulant effects Practice example. Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains

questions.teaching_excerpt: Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay. Trafikverket: Vision Zero

# G1 evidence

Verified 12 October 2026. Five essential claims support four questions; no answer conflicts.

## Nollvisionen – tillsammans räddar vi liv

Publisher: Trafikverket. Version: Last updated/reviewed 5 November 2024. [Source](https://bransch.trafikverket.se/for-dig-i-branschen/samarbete-med-branschen/Samarbeten-for-trafiksakerhet/tillsammans-for-nollvisionen/).

Locator: Introductory aim and shared-responsibility principles 1–3. Short excerpt: “På sikt ska ingen dödas eller allvarligt skadas inom vägtransportsystemet”.

Supports: No deaths or serious injuries in the road transport system; shared responsibility of road users and system designers.

Fallback rationale: Preferred agency supplies exact support; no duplicate organisation added.

## Drowsy Driving

Publisher: NHTSA (United States government). Version: Live page; publication date not displayed in retrieved passage. [Source](https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving).

Locator: Tips to Drive Alert: How To Avoid Driving Drowsy item 1; Short-Term Interventions item 1. Short excerpt: “Getting adequate sleep on a daily basis is the only true way”.

Supports: Adequate sleep is fundamental; coffee/energy drinks can give temporary perceived alertness without preventing microsleep in serious sleep deprivation.

Fallback rationale: Exact sleep-remedy and temporary-alertness distinction not located in inspected TS/TRV pages; general physiological advice applies in Sweden; US speeds and recommendations not imported.

## Microsleeps — Module 3, Negative Impacts on Sleep

Publisher: CDC/NIOSH (United States government). Version: Last reviewed 31 March 2020; Module 3, page 3 of 28. [Source](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/work-hour-training-for-nurses/longhours/mod3/03.html).

Locator: Microsleeps definition. Short excerpt: “involuntary episodes of sleep lasting a few seconds”.

Supports: Brief unintended sleep; general physiological definition, not an occupational driving rule.

Fallback rationale: Exact definition not located in inspected TS/TRV material; proposed VTI lead did not yield a retrievable exact definition.

## Drograttfylleri och sjöfylleri — proposition 1998/99:43

Publisher: Swedish Government; published by Sveriges riksdag. Version: Proposition 1998/99:43. [Source](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/proposition/drograttfylleri-och-sjofylleri_gm0343/html/).

Locator: Printed page 24, paragraph beginning De centralstimulerande medlen. Short excerpt: “kan framkalla påtagligt höjt självförtroende i förening med hyperaktivitet”.

Supports: Amphetamine/cocaine can increase confidence while concentration and clear thinking are impaired.

Fallback rationale: TRV alcohol/drug overview and TS substance reports give general impairment background but not this exact confidence claim. Historical passage used only for physiological effects, never current legal rules or obsolete warning-label advice.

## Drugs and Human Performance Fact Sheets

Publisher: NHTSA (United States government). Version: DOT HS 809 725, April 2004. [Source](https://www.nhtsa.gov/sites/nhtsa.gov/files/809725-drugshumanperformfs.pdf).

Locator: Printed pages 62–64 (PDF pages 63–65), Methamphetamine, Effects / Performance Effects / Effects on Driving. Short excerpt: “reduced fatigue or drowsiness, increased alertness”.

Supports: Perceived fatigue can diminish while risk-taking and driving impairment remain; fatigue and sleepiness may follow as drug effects change.

Fallback rationale: Exact masking claim not located in inspected TS/TRV sources. Historical pharmacology summary supports a qualified can statement about stimulant misuse, not every prescribed dose or every stimulant.

Search log, individual claims and applicability limits: evidence.json. Historical drug-effect documents support physiology only, never current legal rules. The 90 km/h × 2 second = 50 m example is explicitly hypothetical original arithmetic.

G1/proposed-additions.md.text:
# G1 implemented teaching additions

Approved execution: G1 only. Existing chapter styles and artwork reused; no new design required.

Chapter opening: short Vision Zero definition (situation-129).

M01-L02 before Worked decision: microsleep definition and hypothetical 50 m calculation (068); sleep remedy versus temporary alertness (069); qualified stimulant-confidence/masked-fatigue explanation (062); Lina practice example; expanded answered knowledge check.

M01-L03 before Worked decision: Vision Zero explanation and decision example (129); expanded answered knowledge check.

**Medical explanation · Sleep and awareness.** Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts. [CDC/NIOSH: microsleeps][microsleep]

**Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep.** Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See M07-L03 for planning around fatigue on a journey. [NHTSA: drowsy driving][drowsy-driving]

**Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement.** Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving. [Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement][stimulant-confidence] · [NHTSA: stimulant effects][stimulant-fatigue]

**Practice example.** Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains unresolved, and a stronger feeling of alertness cannot certify safe judgement. She postpones the drive or arranges an alert driver, and makes time for adequate sleep before driving again.

**Official policy aim · Vision Zero.** Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay. [Trafikverket: Vision Zero][vision-zero]

Chapter 10 grows from **23 to 24 pages (+1)**, meeting the one-page budget. References retain three pages; four lessons, existing styles and artwork remain. No new design or chapter.

M10-L01 explains residual cooling-system heat and pressure even after switching off. Opening a hot cap can release scalding liquid or steam and cause severe burns. Never open while hot. Follow the actual vehicle handbook; no fixed waiting time, cap-opening sequence, refill procedure or exposed roadside repair instruction. G10/proposed-additions.md.text:
# G10 implemented addition

M10-L01 only. Existing text styles and approved illustrations reused; no new design.

**Overheating · Leave the hot cap closed.** In a conventional pressurised cooling system, hot coolant and steam can remain under pressure even after the engine is switched off. Opening the radiator cap, or the cap of a pressurised coolant reservoir, can release that pressure and expel scalding liquid or steam, causing severe burns. Never loosen or remove the cap while the engine or cooling system is hot. Switching off is not proof that pressure and heat have disappeared. [Manufacturer handbook: hot coolant and pressure warning][hot-coolant]

Treat a temperature warning as a reason to respond according to the actual vehicle handbook, not as an invitation to open a cap. Revisit M02-L01 for warning indicators and fault recognition. Protect people from traffic first and arrange professional assistance where needed. Cooling-system layouts and stopping instructions vary; this lesson gives no fixed waiting time, cap-opening sequence or roadside refill procedure. [Manufacturer cooling-system precautions][hot-coolant] · [Trafikverket: protect people and call recovery][breakdown]

**Apply the warning.** The temperature warning appears on a motorway journey. After reaching the safest available stopping place as conditions allow, follow the vehicle's stopping instructions and this lesson's motorway scene-safety advice. A passenger suggests opening the coolant cap immediately because the engine is now off. Reject that action: residual heat and pressure can still cause a burn. Call recovery from a protected position rather than attempting an exposed repair. If the event is in a tunnel, use the tunnel response above; smoke, fire or danger to life requires the urgent response, not waiting beside the vehicle to diagnose it. [Trafikverket: motorway breakdown][breakdown] · [Trafikverket: tunnel urgency][tunnel]

**Knowledge check.** (1) Is one identical waiting rule suitable for every breakdown? (2) Why must you leave a hot coolant cap closed even after switching off the engine? **Answer:** (1) No. Apply the guidance for the location and urgency, with people’s safety first. (2) Heat and pressure can remain; opening the cap can release scalding coolant or steam and cause severe burns. Do not open it while hot. Follow the actual handbook and arrange assistance; no fixed waiting time proves it safe.

questions.question_prompt: What is a dangerous effect of stimulant drugs on driving?

questions.coverage_reasoning: Overconfidence and reduced perceived fatigue are separately explained and qualified to stimulant misuse; perceived alertness is explicitly distinguished from safe judgement.

questions.question_prompt: What is microsleep in driving?
questions.keyed_answer: A brief unintended episode of sleep.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit definition supports the answer. Hypothetical 90 km/h × 2 seconds = 50 metres demonstrates distance without assigning a typical duration.

questions.question_prompt: What is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation?
questions.keyed_answer: Adequate sleep.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains why coffee, music, an open window and willpower do not replace missing sleep; practice example selects another driver or postponement.

questions.question_prompt: What is the central aim of Vision Zero?
questions.keyed_answer: No one should be killed or seriously injured in road traffic.
questions.coverage_reasoning: States the exact aim and explains the shared responsibility of road users and system designers, with a pressured-overtake example.

questions.question_prompt: What is the safety purpose of a correctly adjusted head restraint?
questions.keyed_answer: To reduce damaging head movement in a collision.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Purpose, relative head movement and adjustment taught; no injury-prevention guarantee.

questions.question_prompt: Why are rear-facing restraints recommended for young children?
questions.keyed_answer: They support the head and neck and distribute crash forces.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains the relatively heavy head/vulnerable neck, simultaneous support and distribution of collision load.

questions.question_prompt: The steering wheel vibrates at certain speeds. Which fault is a possible cause?

questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains rotating uneven mass and possible speed-dependent steering vibration; other causes and assessment retained.

questions.question_prompt: You fit a temporary spare wheel after a puncture. What should guide its use?
questions.keyed_answer: The vehicle's limits for speed, distance and pressure.
questions.coverage_reasoning: All three required limits/use conditions taught; actual handbook controls and no universal number invented.

questions.question_prompt: Why does a car have separate brake circuits?
questions.keyed_answer: To retain some braking if one circuit fails.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Retained partial braking after a circuit fault explained; reduced capability and limits made explicit.

questions.question_prompt: During an emergency stop, your ABS brake pedal pulsates. What should you normally do?
questions.keyed_answer: Maintain firm pressure and steer as needed.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Normal ABS pulsation is distinguished from abnormal ordinary pedal behaviour; firm pressure, no pumping and steering taught.

questions.question_prompt: The brake pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure. What should you suspect?
questions.keyed_answer: A potentially serious brake-system leak or fault.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Serious possible hydraulic fault explained; professional assessment rather than definitive symptom diagnosis.

questions.question_prompt: A hydraulic brake pedal feels unusually springy. What may be wrong?
questions.keyed_answer: Air in the brake system.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Air in hydraulic brakes is linked to unusual springiness/sponginess with appropriate action.

questions.question_prompt: Why are parts of a car designed to deform in a crash?
questions.keyed_answer: To absorb energy and reduce the forces reaching occupants.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains energy absorption, protected passenger space, longer deceleration and lower occupant forces.

questions.question_prompt: What is the purpose of an electrical fuse?
questions.keyed_answer: To protect a circuit against excessive current.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Circuit protection against overload/short circuit taught; maritime source used only for common electrical principle.

questions.question_prompt: How do you use the three-second following-distance guideline?
questions.keyed_answer: Count the time between the car ahead and your car passing the same fixed point.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains the fixed-point/rear-to-front counting method, a three-second guideline, smooth gap adjustment and conditions requiring more space.

questions.question_prompt: A car follows you too closely. How can you reduce the risk?
questions.keyed_answer: Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead and avoid sudden braking.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Teaches increasing forward space so slowing/braking can be gentler; tailgater example and emergency-braking boundary included.

questions.question_prompt: With otherwise identical grip and braking, what happens to braking distance when speed doubles?
questions.keyed_answer: It becomes approximately four times as long.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains 2× speed → 4× braking distance under identical deceleration assumptions; reaction distance and total stopping distance are explicitly distinguished and arithmetic checked.

questions.question_prompt: You must wait before turning left across oncoming traffic. How should you hold your front wheels?
questions.keyed_answer: Keep them straight until you can turn.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicitly teaches front wheels straight while stopped before a left turn across oncoming traffic, the rear-impact/oncoming-path risk, and beginning steering only when the movement is safe. Classified as safety advice; example and answered check reinforce the distinction.

questions.question_prompt: The speed limit is 70 km/h and a bus signals to leave its stop. Which statement is correct?
questions.keyed_answer: The bus must give way, but you should still be ready to cooperate.
questions.coverage_reasoning: All three essential claims taught: ≤50 special opportunity/stop duty, safe bus entry at 70, and continued cooperation under §43. Explicitly distinguishes road limit from actual speed; original 40 km/h bus example extended to a 70 km/h comparison.

questions.question_prompt: How should you behave around a guide dog working in traffic?
questions.keyed_answer: Avoid distracting it.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Avoids attention directed at the working dog; explains handler risk, communication with handler and a guide-dog interaction example.

questions.question_prompt: Which road user is operating a vehicle under the traffic definitions?
questions.keyed_answer: A person riding a bicycle.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit ordinary-pedal-bicycle vehicle definition and rider operating a vehicle, distinguished from motor vehicle terminology; existing crossing duties cross-referenced.

questions.question_prompt: After a long motorway drive, 60 km/h feels unusually slow. What should you do?
questions.keyed_answer: Check the speedometer and adapt to the new road conditions.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains steady-speed perceptual adaptation, deceptive slow feeling, speedometer checks, current limit/conditions and motorway-to-50 example. Feeling alone does not establish instrument fault.

questions.question_prompt: Heavy traffic makes a country-road left turn unsafe. What is a sensible alternative?
questions.keyed_answer: Continue to a suitable turning place and return for a right turn.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Teaches continuing to a suitable permitted turnaround/place or return route, returning for a safe right turn, legal boundaries, no immediate unsafe turnaround, and choosing another route if no suitable return exists. Conditional editorial inference from official rerouting example and Swedish rules is disclosed in evidence.

questions.question_prompt: When is extra attention to large animals especially important?
questions.keyed_answer: Around dusk and dawn near wildlife habitats and fence openings.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit dawn/dusk, habitat edges/bushes/waterways and fence endings/openings, with observation and speed-planning example; year-round uncertainty retained and post-collision instructions cross-linked to M10.

questions.question_prompt: May you use dipped headlights and front fog lights together?
questions.keyed_answer: No.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Names the Swedish prohibited pair explicitly and explains replacement in fog/heavy precipitation.

questions.question_prompt: Which task relies particularly on central vision?
questions.keyed_answer: Reading the precise wording on a road sign.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Defines central detail vision and its role in reading exact sign wording.

questions.question_prompt: Why is peripheral vision important in traffic?
questions.keyed_answer: It helps detect movement and potential hazards outside your direct focus.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains peripheral detection outside direct focus and eye/head movement for direct inspection, with verge example.

questions.question_prompt: You see one light approaching at night. What should you remember?
questions.keyed_answer: It may be a wider vehicle with a failed headlight.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains possible wider car with failed lamp and clearance caution; conditional editorial inference from documented defective car lamps.

questions.question_prompt: Why can a bridge freeze before nearby road sections?
questions.keyed_answer: Cold air can cool it from above and below.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains exposed bridge cooling and possible earlier freezing, not an always-first guarantee.

questions.question_prompt: Rain falls near freezing temperature onto a cold road. What risk should you anticipate?
questions.keyed_answer: A nearly invisible slippery ice layer.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit freezing on sufficiently cold surface, thin deceptive ice and distinction between air and road temperature.

questions.question_prompt: After a long dry spell, the first rain begins. What should you consider?
questions.keyed_answer: Dirt and residues can make the surface unusually slippery.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains accumulation and mixing by first rain, reduced grip and no guaranteed cleaning time.

questions.question_prompt: Why are the tyres with the best grip generally fitted on the rear axle?
questions.keyed_answer: To reduce the risk of the rear losing grip and swinging out.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains rear stability, tail slide and rotation risk behind the best-rear-tyre recommendation.

questions.question_prompt: What happens in oversteer?
questions.keyed_answer: The rear loses grip and the car turns more than intended.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Defines the grip-loss oversteer case: rear slide and excess rotation.

questions.question_prompt: What happens in understeer?
questions.keyed_answer: The front loses grip and the car turns less than intended.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Defines grip-loss understeer: front saturation, reduced turn and straighter/wider path; distinguishes ordinary handling characteristics.

questions.question_prompt: What occurs during aquaplaning?
questions.keyed_answer: Water prevents the tyre from maintaining proper contact with the road.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains water-supported tyre film and reduced/absent effective road contact, steering/braking limits.

questions.question_prompt: Your car starts aquaplaning. What is the appropriate response?
questions.keyed_answer: Ease off the accelerator and avoid abrupt steering or braking.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Both essential responses: gradual accelerator release and avoiding abrupt steering/braking, with gentle necessary corrections. Cross-link to M02-L01 ABS and scope excludes universal never-brake instruction.

questions.question_prompt: A light lorry has no trailer. Which maximum speed generally applies?
questions.keyed_answer: The speed limit of the road, subject to safe adaptation.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains light-lorry ≤3500 kg road-maximum treatment without trailer, contrast with heavy-lorry caps, lower road limits, safe adaptation and towing exception; includes signed-100 example.

questions.question_prompt: A trailer presses too heavily down on the towball. What can happen?
questions.keyed_answer: The car's front axle can be unloaded, impairing steering grip.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Defines coupling force distinct from total trailer weight; rear coupling leverage unloads front axle and impairs steering grip. Explains not necessarily lifting wheels off road, actual limits and forward-load example.

questions.question_prompt: What normally happens if the required inspection deadline is missed?
questions.keyed_answer: An automatic driving ban applies until the inspection requirements are addressed.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit automatic missed-deadline ban, owner responsibility without reminder, booking not enough, legal endpoint when inspection performed and further-result constraints. Includes correct on/off-road exceptions, insurance/tax requirements, dangerous-defect distinction and 31-October/1-November example.

questions.question_prompt: Why does burning fossil petrol contribute to climate change?
questions.keyed_answer: It adds carbon dioxide from long-stored carbon to the atmosphere.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Long-stored fossil carbon combines with oxygen, releases CO₂ and strengthens natural greenhouse effect.

questions.question_prompt: When is a conventional catalytic converter least effective?
questions.keyed_answer: Just after a cold engine is started.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Conventional petrol three-way catalyst needs sufficient heat, so cold-start effectiveness is low; no universal warm-up duration.

questions.question_prompt: Does a catalytic converter remove the climate impact of burning fossil fuel?
questions.keyed_answer: No, fossil carbon dioxide emissions remain.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Pollutant conversion distinguished from continued fossil CO₂/climate effect; catalyst is not carbon capture.

questions.question_prompt: Why use a timer with an engine heater?
questions.keyed_answer: To warm the engine when needed without wasting electricity.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Timer schedules needed heating and avoids unnecessarily long electricity use; actual equipment/conditions govern duration.

questions.question_prompt: How can you use air conditioning sensibly?
questions.keyed_answer: Use it as needed for comfort, alertness and clear windows without unnecessary cooling.
questions.coverage_reasoning: All three claims: energy demand, comfort/alertness, and clear-window demisting. Avoid needless cooling while retaining safety; cooling does not cure sleep deprivation.

questions.question_prompt: Where is the environmentally preferable place to wash a car?
questions.keyed_answer: A purpose-built wash facility that treats wastewater.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Wastewater collection/treatment linked to oil, metals and chemicals; compatible products/local rules, no zero-pollution promise.

questions.question_prompt: What is a major danger of carbon monoxide?
questions.keyed_answer: It interferes with the blood's oxygen transport.
questions.coverage_reasoning: CO binding to haemoglobin prevents normal oxygen transport; kept distinct from CO₂.

questions.question_prompt: Which environmental problem is associated with nitrogen oxides from traffic?
questions.keyed_answer: Airway irritation and contributions to acidification and ground-level ozone.
questions.coverage_reasoning: NOx airway irritation, acidification, ground-level ozone formation with hydrocarbons/sunlight all individually evidenced.

questions.question_prompt: Why are traffic particles a health concern?
questions.keyed_answer: They can harm the respiratory system.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Exhaust/wear particles can enter airways and cause respiratory harm.

questions.question_prompt: In a manual car, which gear choice generally saves fuel without straining the engine?
questions.keyed_answer: Use a suitably high gear while the engine runs smoothly.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Conventional manual-car high gear conditional on smooth unstrained operation; load/gradient may require lower gear.

questions.question_prompt: What is engine braking in a conventional manual car?
questions.keyed_answer: Slowing with the accelerator released while a suitable gear remains engaged.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Accelerator released, suitable gear engaged; clutch/neutral disengagement not this technique; necessary braking and vehicle-specific behaviour retained.

questions.question_prompt: Which statement about an electric car is accurate?
questions.keyed_answer: It has no tailpipe exhaust while driving, but production and energy supply still have impacts.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Battery-electric electricity-only propulsion implies no combustion exhaust while driving; manufacturing, extraction and electricity supply still affect environment.

questions.question_prompt: What distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from a conventional non-plug-in hybrid?
questions.keyed_answer: Its traction battery can be charged from an external electricity supply.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Plug-in externally rechargeable contrasted with non-plug-in hybrid not externally rechargeable.

questions.question_prompt: Why can cities restrict studded tyres on particular roads?
questions.keyed_answer: Studs contribute to road wear and airborne particles.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Stud wear → particles → airway harm; municipality can restrict road/area. Check STFS dates/extent/exceptions/signs, national season does not override local ban, correct C44 exception and cross-link M07-L02.

questions.question_prompt: What should you do with heavy equipment you no longer need in the car?
questions.keyed_answer: Remove it before future journeys.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Remove unneeded heavy cargo before trips, distinct from roof-box drag; retain needed safety/access equipment.

questions.question_prompt: The engine has overheated. Why should you not immediately open a hot coolant cap?
questions.keyed_answer: Pressurised hot coolant or steam can cause burns.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explicit residual heat/pressure even engine off, cap opening expels scalding fluid/steam causing burns; never open while hot. Vehicle handbook and M02-L01 warning cross-link; worked motorway decision with tunnel urgency distinction, no fixed wait or repair sequence.

G12/completion.md.text:
# G12 final question coverage review

Completed 13 October 2026. All **1000 records** were rechecked against the verified **540-page revised PDF**. All **55 targeted driving-situation gaps** have actual printed teaching and **68 source-linked essential claims**. No question-bank or PDF changes were made by G12.

| Result | Original 498-page book | Revised 540-page book | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Covered by book study | 697 | **772** | +75 |
| Missing teaching/illustration | 233 | **158** | −75 |
| Prompt-only calculations | 70 | **70** | 0 |
| Total without adequate book teaching | 303 | **228** | −75 |

The gain includes **55 situation questions plus 20 braking-factor exercises** supported by G3's printed square-of-speed explanation. All 178 situation questions are supported under the stated criterion. No previously covered question lost support.

## Deliverables and numbering

- [Covered questions with final book pages](../../question-page-map.json): 772 records, retaining prompts, options, keyed answers, category and evidence.
- [Remaining gaps](../../question-coverage-gaps.json): all 228 missing/prompt-only records with precise reasons.
- [Complete audit](../../all-question-coverage.json): all 1000 questions in original order.
- [55-target printed evidence and claim links](target-coverage-review.json).
- [Reviewed scenario decisions](scenario-decisions.json), [arithmetic verification](arithmetic-validation.json), [coverage changes](coverage-changes.json) and [validation](validation.json).

`book_pages` and `primary_book_page` use one-based physical PDF pages, including the cover; continuous visible folios and PDF labels agree. `original_source_page` preserves the old bank field and is not a page in this book. All generated decisions are bound to the final PDF/bank hashes. The reusable audit script now checks evidence and actual component placement rather than reusing old hard-coded scenario statuses and page numbers.

All targets passed fresh printed-phrase checks, individual required-claim linkage and full relevant-page review. The original claims' legal, vehicle and condition limits remain. Independent audit checks were not replaced by simply marking all target IDs covered.

## Remaining gaps

**79 absent sign codes** cause **158 meaning/recognition gaps**. Existing illustrated entries were verified by exact code, caption text and official asset placement; a family overview, code lookup or external link is insufficient. [Missing-code and question list](missing-signs.json).

**30 rough stopping-distance questions** supply their own reaction formula and 0.4 braking coefficient. The new book teaches exact unit conversion, speed-squared scaling and a different explicitly assumed deceleration example, not those rough-model coefficients. They remain prompt-only. **40 fuel/use-savings questions** likewise supply enough numbers for proportional arithmetic without a taught fuel-calculation method. These families require separate teaching additions if all 1000 questions must be answerable from study.

## Checks and practical limits

All 178 scenarios reviewed against actual supporting pages, with six remapped/expanded-page cases inspected specifically. Stronger explicit passages were selected where appropriate, including the railway emergency answer p.228 and new hybrid teaching p.292. All 616 sign records checked by exact illustrated entries; all 206 numerical instances independently recalculated from the actual prompt figures and checked against keyed answers. Every ID occurs once, all page references exist, the covered/gap partition is disjoint and complete, and all question fields/original order remain.

The criterion is **selecting the keyed answer**, not reproducing every explanation or every clause of a keyed answer. Questions 081, 087, 151 and 175 explicitly record applications of core printed principles and limits on extra keyed detail (for example, individual-wheel braking is not itself explained, although stability control's stabilising function distinguishes the correct choice). This is a curriculum coverage audit, not a new legal/medical certification.

One non-blocking editorial correction: M06-L01 on p.191 points wildlife-collision actions to M10-L01; those actions are in **M10-L02, p.326**. Q126's prevention teaching and q127's collision response remain supported by their correct mapped passages. [Observation](editorial-observations.json). The G11 PDF is preserved; no extra editorial changes were folded into G12.

Reproducible replay passes. Representative full-size pages 84, 85 and 443 reviewed; G11's full-page component comparison and affected-page visual checks remain evidence. Question bank, book, delivery copy and ten chapter PDFs stayed byte-identical; all **154 G0 snapshots** verified. Original audit files remain in those snapshots, and the original audit code is also saved in G12.

Book SHA-256: `c21ea3887b3f67bfd40a5683908df990187432a035d025898e7f0700380fa299`.

Question-bank SHA-256: `303519698e564c9fb9aa835a29acd743d2038bca54be87cc71efd11951c4a3bb`.

## Plan completion

**G0–G12 complete for the approved 55-gap plan.** Remaining 228 bank records are explicitly listed; filling them is a further curriculum scope, not part of the completed chapter-gap plan. Publication/app migration, print masters and full tagged-PDF accessibility approval remain separate.

These are **local Chapter 2 pages**, not final book page numbers. [Question/page JSON](coverage.json) includes sources, evidence links and coverage reasoning for each question.

Chapter 2 grows from **15 to 19 pages (+4)**, within the planned 3–4 pages. Two additional teaching pages cover braking/electrical protection and occupant/crash protection; two additional reference pages accommodate the verified sources. Tyre/spare teaching fits the existing lesson page. Four lessons remain; no additional chapter. Existing artwork, type sizes and reusable table style retained; no new visual design required.

M02-L01 adds separate brake circuits, normal emergency ABS feedback, a symptom/possible cause/action table, hydraulic fault recognition and fuse function. M02-L02 adds wheel imbalance and vehicle-specific temporary-spare limits, plus a practice example. M02-L03 explains head-restraint protection, rear-facing support and controlled crash deformation. Expanded comprehension checks have reasoning on a separate answer page. M02-L04 and the review text remain unchanged. Handling and hot-coolant cross-references added.

Transportstyrelsen/Trafikverket provide direct support for head restraints, child protection, brake circuits, sinking-pedal inspection and the general fuse principle. The fuse source is maritime guidance and is used solely for the common electrical principle, never as car-installation law. Where precise agency support was not located, official fallbacks are Northern Ireland's driver manual (wheel balance/air in hydraulic brakes), UK Government Rule 120 (ABS action), and Western Australia's Road Safety Commission (crumple zones). Manufacturer passages supplement only the vehicle-specific spare instructions (2019 Volvo V60 Twin Engine) and normal ABS pulsation (2011 Ford Explorer). No foreign driving rules or universal spare speed/distance are imported. See [evidence](evidence.md) for versions, locators, search limits and original explanatory inferences.

The question bank, both 498-page review PDFs, all G0 snapshots and Chapter 1 PDF remain unchanged. M01 and M03–M10 manuscript teaching is unchanged. The tracker has also been reconciled with the existing passed G1 completion records; no G1 content was altered.

questions.keyed_answer: To retain some braking if one circuit fails.
questions.teaching_excerpt: Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. questions.coverage_reasoning: Retained partial braking after a circuit fault explained; reduced capability and limits made explicit.

questions.question_prompt: During an emergency stop, your ABS brake pedal pulsates. What should you normally do?
questions.keyed_answer: Maintain firm pressure and steer as needed.
questions.teaching_excerpt: keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer Recognise a symptom, then act. questions.question_prompt: Why are parts of a car designed to deform in a crash?
questions.keyed_answer: To absorb energy and reduce the forces reaching occupants.
questions.teaching_excerpt: Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. # G2 implemented additions

G2 approval covers Chapter 2 only. Existing text pages, reusable reference-table style and approved artwork reused. No new visual design required.

## M02-L01

**Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection.** Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. [Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits][brake-circuits]

**ABS in an emergency.** Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. [UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120][abs-driving] · [Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer][abs-feedback]

**Recognise a symptom, then act.** The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change. [Transportstyrelsen: brake inspection][brake-inspection] · [Northern Ireland government: vehicle faults][vehicle-faults]

| Symptom | Possible cause | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Pulsating pedal during an emergency ABS stop | Normal ABS operation | Keep firm continuous pressure; steer as needed. |
| Pedal slowly sinks under steady pressure | Hydraulic leakage or another brake fault | Do not start an unsafe journey; obtain professional help. |
| Hydraulic pedal feels unusually springy or spongy | Air in the brake system | Have it checked before moving; do not rely on normal braking. |
| Steering vibrates at certain speeds | Wheel imbalance; other faults are possible | Have tyres, wheels and steering assessed; see M02-L02. |

**What a fuse does.** A fuse protects an electrical circuit by interrupting excessive current during an overload or short circuit. Investigate faults under the actual vehicle's instructions. [Transportstyrelsen: fuse protection principle][fuse-protection]

## M02-L02

**Technical explanation · Steering vibration.** Uneven mass distribution around a rotating wheel and tyre can cause steering vibration, sometimes most noticeable at particular speeds. Wheel imbalance is one possible cause, not a diagnosis: tyre damage and other wheel or steering defects may also be involved. Arrange assessment rather than testing the symptom by driving faster. [Northern Ireland government: wheel balance and vehicle faults][vehicle-faults]

**Vehicle instructions · A temporary spare.** Before using a temporary spare, read the actual car and spare-wheel instructions for maximum speed, distance or use restrictions, and required tyre pressure. Follow those limits and replace it with the normal wheel as instructed. Its pressure can differ from the road tyres. Volvo's 2019 V60 Twin Engine handbook gives one model's temporary-use, speed and pressure requirements; these cannot be assumed for every car. [Volvo: temporary spare, 2019 V60 Twin Engine][temporary-spare]

**Practice example.** Omar notices vibration on a journey and proposes fitting an unfamiliar temporary spare. He first obtains help to assess the symptom, then checks whether the spare is suitable and reads its limits. Changing a wheel does not establish the original cause. Handling and grip are developed in M07-L02. For hot-coolant precautions during other vehicle checks, see M10-L01.

## M02-L03

**Technical explanation · Head restraints.** In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. [Trafikverket: seats and head restraints][seats]

**Why children face backwards.** A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility. [Trafikverket: child head and neck protection][child-advice] · [Transportstyrelsen: rear-facing collision protection][child-rules]

**Controlled deformation.** Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. [Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones][crumple-zones]

**Practice example.** A family prepares a car for a child and an adult passenger. They check rear-facing seat fit and airbag compatibility, and adjust the adult's head restraint. After discussing crash protection, they recognise that the restraint, seat and deforming vehicle structure have different roles that work together.

Expanded lesson knowledge checks have separate answers. Four lessons retained; M02-L04 unchanged.

# G3 completed — Chapter 3

Completed 12 October 2026. All three assigned questions have sourced teaching, examples and answered comprehension checks in M03-L04. Three essential claims verified; no keyed-answer conflict found.

| Question | Topic | Teaching page | Check page | Answer page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| situation-106 | Fixed-point three-second gap method | 44 | 46 | 49 |
| situation-107 | Increase forward space when tailgated | 45 | 46 | 49 |
| situation-138 | Doubled speed / fourfold braking distance | 45 | 46 | 49 |

These are **local Chapter 3 page numbers**, not final book pages. [Question/page JSON](coverage.json) records each question, its keyed answer, teaching excerpt, evidence and coverage reasoning.

Chapter 3 grows from **50 to 52 pages (+2)**, meeting the two-page budget. One new teaching page and one new reference page; the fixed-point material fits an existing learning page. Four lessons retained, with no additional chapter or new diagram. Existing page styles, artwork, all 100 official sign placements and their positions are unchanged. The reference-page destination naming was extended to give the new third reference page a unique destination.

The teaching explains fixed-point selection, counting from the leading car passing it until your car arrives, and a worked counting example. Three seconds is advice, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee. A tailgater example explains why more room ahead allows gentler slowing; necessary emergency braking remains necessary.

Trafikverket's VGU 2024:148, printed page 9, supplies the braking-distance equation. The original derivation fixes deceleration/gradient and sets final speed to zero: d = v²/(2a), so doubled speed gives fourfold braking distance. Real grip and braking can vary. A hypothetical 40/80 km/h example, constant 5 m/s² deceleration and one-second delay gives braking distances 12.3/49.4 m, reaction distances 11.1/22.2 m and totals 23.5/71.6 m. The total does not quadruple. Original unit-conversion teaching remains.

Precise TS/TRV passages for the timed method and tailgater response were not located in the documented searches. Appropriate official fallbacks: Transport for NSW's fixed-point method and Northern Ireland's government driver manual, page 83, for forward-gap/gentler-braking advice. Only common techniques are used; foreign driving laws and numerical reaction-time assumptions are not imported. The Swedish following-distance rule, Traffic Regulation chapter 3 §2, was separately rechecked. See [evidence](evidence.md). The VGU equation was inspected through its complete indexed primary-PDF passage; direct PDF retrieval timed out. Publication identity is confirmed by Trafikverket's current VGU overview. No downloaded-source checksum is claimed.

Validation passed: all manuscript blocks, source links, internal navigation, embedded fonts, text bounds, approved artwork/official sign hashes, separated answers and reproducible build. Arithmetic independently checked. All 52 rendered pages inspected, with full-size detail checks on 44, 45, 49, 51 and 52. [Validation](validation.json).

The question bank, both 498-page review PDFs, all 154 G0 snapshots and every other chapter PDF remain unchanged. Other modules, M03-L01–L03 and the review text are unchanged. G1–G3 now teach **17 of 55 gaps**; **38 remain** for G4–G10. Final book assembly/pagination and the whole-bank audit await G11/G12. G4 has not been executed.

# G3 evidence

Verified 12 October 2026: three essential claims for three questions.

## Safe stopping distance

Transport for NSW / NSW Government (Australia). Live guidance; publication date not displayed in inspected passage. [Source](https://www.nsw.gov.au/driving-boating-and-transport/driving-nsw/roads-safety-and-rules/safe-driving/safe-stopping-distance).

Locator: Working out your crash avoidance space, steps 1–3; video transcript general-rule explanation. Short excerpt: “count how long it takes you to pass the same object as the vehicle in front of you”.

Support: Select a fixed roadside point; count three seconds between lead vehicle and own vehicle passing it; increase margins for poor conditions.

Scope: Technique only. Three seconds is presented as a guideline, not a Swedish statutory interval or universal guarantee. Australian reaction-time assumptions, long-vehicle laws, penalty rules and left-side placement instructions are not imported.

Retrieval: Direct primary page retrieved and inspected

Fallback: Exact fixed-point/counting instruction not located in targeted TS/TRV or Swedish-agency searches. Trafikverket-hosted NESTA and tunnel reports mention a three-second guideline but do not teach the counting method. Official NSW guidance supplies the exact technique.

## Taxi Driver Manual

Department for Infrastructure / Driver & Vehicle Agency, Northern Ireland government. Version 2.1 March 2024; hosted file August 2025. [Source](https://www.northernireland.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2025-08/taxi-manual-august-2025.pdf).

Locator: Printed/PDF p.83: Tailgating (zero-based PDF index 82). Short excerpt: “gradually reduce your speed to increase the gap between you and any vehicle ahead”.

Support: When followed too closely, gradually enlarge the forward gap to allow gentler braking and reduce rear-impact risk.

Scope: Common defensive-driving advice only, not Northern Ireland taxi law. Risk reduction is not a guarantee; necessary emergency braking remains necessary. Its two-second target is not imported.

Retrieval: Direct primary PDF retrieved and inspected

Fallback: Exact increase-forward-gap/gentler-braking behavioural instruction not located in inspected TS/TRV material. This government manual provides the explicit causal advice.

## KRAV Grundvärden, Vägar och gators utformning (VGU)

Trafikverket. TRV publication 2024:148, version 1.0; recognised by current Trafikverket VGU overview as part of current framework. [Source](https://trafikverket.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2%3A1909331/FULLTEXT01.pdf).

Locator: Printed p.9(58): braking-distance equation and variable definitions. Short excerpt: “Bromssträckan erhålls enligt formeln”.

Support: S_b = (V1² − V2²) / [2g(f_b + i)]; setting final speed to zero and holding denominator constant establishes the speed-squared braking-distance relationship.

Scope: Original mathematical derivation from agency equation. Hold grip/braking deceleration and gradient constant; real design friction can depend on speed. No general promise of exact fourfold road-test distance or fourfold total stopping distance.

Retrieval: Complete indexed primary-PDF equation passage retrieved through search. Direct PDF opens timed out; no local source download or checksum claimed.

# G3 implemented teaching additions

Approved scope: M03-L04 only. Existing text-page design and artwork reused; no new diagram or visual design required. A mathematical relationship is stated in ordinary text.

**Safety advice · Check a timed gap.** For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. [NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method][following-gap]

**Fixed-point example.** The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye.

**Safety advice · When someone follows too closely.** Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. [Northern Ireland government: tailgater response][vehicle-faults]

**Tailgater example.** Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop.

**Physical explanation · Twice the speed.** With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: **2 × speed → 4 × braking distance**. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. [Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation][braking-model]

**Hypothetical comparison.** Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does **not** quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car.

**Knowledge check.** (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? **Answer:** (1) It doubles under the constant-speed assumption. (2) Count seconds from the rear of the car ahead passing a fixed point until your front reaches that point; three seconds is a guideline and conditions may require more. (3) More forward space allows gentler slowing and gives the follower more time; avoid unnecessary sudden braking. (4) Braking distance becomes approximately four times as long, but reaction distance doubles for the same response delay, so the combined total does not generally quadruple.

# G4 implemented additions

Approved scope: M04-L02 only. Existing text-page style and approved artwork reused; no new diagram or visual design needed.

**Safety advice · Wait with front wheels straight.** When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it. [New York DMV: waiting to turn left][left-turn-wheels]

**Waiting is different from turning.** Follow the positioning, signalling and observation requirements above. The wheel-position advice does not create permission to enter or block a junction, ignore a signal, or obstruct someone else's path. Continue observing oncoming traffic, the receiving road, crossings and vehicles behind you while waiting. Recheck the full path before moving.

**Practice example.** Sami is stopped in a suitable position, signalling left while oncoming cars pass. A passenger suggests turning the wheels left now to be ready. Sami keeps them straight: preparing the intention is different from starting the movement. Once the gap and receiving road permit a safe turn, he moves and steers into it. On rural roads, use M06-L01 to assess bends, crests and other risks before choosing a turning opportunity.

**Knowledge check.** (1) Does a driver in the continuing lane have no responsibility when someone is merging? (2) You are stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic. Which way should the front wheels point, why, and when should you start steering into the turn? **Answer:** (1) No. They must adapt speed to facilitate an observed entry; the joining driver must still make a safe movement. (2) Keep the front wheels straight while waiting. Pre-turning them left can direct the car into oncoming traffic if it is struck from behind. Begin steering into the turn only when the movement can be made safely; a signal alone does not establish that opportunity.

M06-L01 is cross-referenced for existing rural-risk assessment. Detailed rural left-turn alternatives remain G6 work; no M06 teaching changed.

G5/evidence.md.text:
# G5 evidence

Checked 13 October 2026. Five essential claims for three questions.

## Traffic Regulation (1998:1276)

Swedish Government; published by Sveriges riksdag. Consolidated live text; chapter 3 §§43–45 checked as applicable 13 October 2026. [Source](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/trafikforordning-19981276_sfs-1998-1276/).

Locator: Chapter 3 §45: maximum permitted road speed ≤50, approaching-driver duty and bus caution; §43: safe edge/lateral movement and facilitating observed lane entry. Short excerpt: “utan fara eller onödigt hinder; anpassa hastigheten så att inkörningen underlättas; 50 kilometer i timmen eller lägre”.

Support: Special bus-stop departure duty at road limits ≤50; no such special duty at 70, but safe-entry and speed-adaptation/cooperation duties remain.

Scope: Ordinary departure from roadside bus stop into the approaching driver’s lane, subject to other applicable controls/rules. Road maximum limit, not actual vehicle speed, determines §45. No unconditional priority or permission to force a gap. “Must give way” in the keyed answer is explained as waiting for a safe entry under §43, not an invented separate always-yield statute.

Fallback: Inspected TS/TRV results did not establish the complete current 50/70 comparison and reciprocal duties. The current statutory provisions give exact primary legal support.

## Fakta om ledarhundar

Myndigheten för delaktighet (MFD). Last updated 30 April 2026. [Source](https://www.mfd.se/ledarhundsverksamheten/fakta-om-ledarhundar/).

Locator: När du möter ett ledarhundsekipage, first and third bullets; Så här arbetar ledarhundar. Short excerpt: “Stör inte ledarhundar som arbetar genom att klappa eller prata med dem.”.

Support: Avoid petting/talking to distract working guide dogs; distraction can endanger handler; communicate with handler, who chooses route and remains in control.

Scope: Safety/interaction advice, not a newly asserted traffic offence. No claim that the dog alone decides a road is safe or every glance necessarily distracts it.

Fallback: No exact guide-dog distraction advice located in TS/TRV searches. MFD is the Swedish government authority responsible for guide-dog services and supplies directly applicable guidance.

## Cykel

Transportstyrelsen. Last updated 16 February 2026. [Source](https://www.transportstyrelsen.se/sv/vagtrafik/fordon/fordonsregler/regler-for-olika-fordonsslag/cykel/).

Locator: Definitionen av en cykel, definition item 1 under Act (2001:559). Short excerpt: “Ett fordon som är avsett att drivas med tramp- eller vevanordning och inte är ett lekfordon.”.

Support: An ordinary pedal bicycle is a vehicle even though not motor-driven; a rider is operating a vehicle.

Scope: Ordinary pedal bicycle, excluding toy vehicles. No unnecessary e-bike/e-scooter taxonomy or implication that every crossing rule is identical for all vehicles.

Fallback: Exact preferred-agency definition; no additional publisher cited.

Individual mappings and source searches: evidence.json. The 70 km/h comparison follows from the §45 threshold and §43 reciprocal duties. No manufacturer or foreign sources are needed.

G5/proposed-additions.md.text:
# G5 implemented additions

Approved scope: M05-L01 only. Existing text and two-column table style and approved artwork reused; no new diagram needed.

**Bus comparison · Check the road limit.** The threshold concerns the maximum permitted speed on the road, not how fast you happen to be travelling. At a 70 km/h limit, the special bus-stop departure rule above does not apply. The bus must wait for an entry that can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. You still have a duty to adapt speed to facilitate an observed entry into your lane. A bus indicator does not create unconditional priority, and the higher road limit does not excuse deliberately blocking it. [Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§43–45][traffic-law]

| Road limit | Duties when the bus signals to leave its stop |
|---|---|
| 50 km/h or lower | Slow and let the bus leave; stop if needed. The bus driver must take particular care. |
| 70 km/h, ordinary entry into your lane | The special bus-exit duty does not apply. The bus waits for a safe entry; you adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry. |

**Safety advice · Let a guide dog work.** Do not pet, call to or talk to a working guide dog to attract its attention. Distraction can endanger the person it is helping. Allow the pair room and time; if you need to communicate, address the handler rather than trying to direct the dog. The handler chooses the route and remains in control. For example, a passenger beside your parked car wants to greet a guide dog at a crossing. Ask them to leave it working and keep the path clear. [MFD: meeting a working guide dog][guide-dog]

**Traffic terminology · A bicycle is a vehicle.** A person riding an ordinary pedal bicycle is operating a vehicle, even without an engine. “Vehicle” does not mean only “motor vehicle”. Apply the relevant cyclist duties and protections; crossing distinctions remain in M04-L03. [Transportstyrelsen: bicycle definition][bicycle-definition]

**Worked decision.** On a 40 km/h street, a bus signals out. You ease speed early and leave room rather than trying to squeeze past. You also watch for people near the stop; making space for the bus is not your only task. Compare an otherwise ordinary 70 km/h road: the bus waits for a safe entry, while you still adapt speed to help an observed entry into your lane. Travelling at 40 on that 70 road does not activate the special bus rule.

**Knowledge check.** (1) Does a narrow visible gap beside a cyclist prove passing is safe? (2) A bus signals from its stop on a 70 km/h road while you drive at 40. Does the special bus rule apply, and what must both drivers do? (3) Should you greet a working guide dog? (4) Is a person riding a pedal bicycle operating a vehicle? **Answer:** (1) No. Consider possible rider movement, obstacles, oncoming traffic and a safe lateral margin; wait if needed. (2) No: the road limit determines the threshold. The bus must enter safely without unnecessary obstruction; you must adapt speed to facilitate the observed entry into your lane. At limits of 50 or lower, slow and let the bus leave, stopping if necessary; the bus driver must take particular care. (3) No. Avoid distracting it by petting, calling or talking to it; communicate with the handler if needed. (4) Yes. A bicycle is a vehicle even without an engine.

# G6 completed — Chapter 6

Completed 13 October 2026. Three assigned gaps have teaching and answered comprehension checks. Three essential claims checked with explicit scope; no keyed-answer conflict found.

| Question | Topic | Teaching page | Check page | Answer page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| situation-075 | Speed perception after prolonged motorway driving | 25 | 27 | 48 |
| situation-105 | Safer approach when a rural left turn is unsafe | 11 | 13 | 48 |
| situation-126 | Wildlife attention: dawn/dusk, habitats, fence openings | 11 | 13 | 48 |

These are **local Chapter 6 pages**, not final book pages. [Question/page JSON](coverage.json) includes original prompts, keyed answers, teaching excerpts, sources and reasoning.

Chapter 6 grows from **48 to 50 pages (+2)**, within the 1–2-page budget. Two teaching pages reuse the existing text style. Ten references fit two pages using five entries each and existing type sizes. No additional chapter, artwork or diagram; all four lessons remain.

M06-L01 explains continuing to a suitable permitted turning place or route and returning for a right turn when a direct left turn is unsafe, including a rural example and explicit safety/legal conditions. The book does not suggest an immediate carriageway turnaround or a turnaround on a motorway/expressway. Wheel-position advice in M04-L02 is cross-linked without implying that it makes an unsafe turn acceptable. Wildlife material adds habitat-edge and fence-opening observation cues and a dusk example; prevention remains separate from M10-L01 collision response.

M06-L03 explains speed adaptation after prolonged steady motorway driving, speedometer checks and a transition to a road signed 50 km/h. Feeling slow alone does not establish speedometer failure or justify accelerating.

**Evidence limits:** Trafikverket supplies exact wildlife timing/fence-opening advice and a project-specific habitat example. It also provides a historical example of rerouting an unavailable left turn to identified turning locations. The general rural return-right alternative is a **conditional editorial planning inference**, not a verbatim national agency recommendation; current Swedish Traffic Regulation constraints are cited separately. Exact TS/TRV/VTI advice covering speed adaptation plus speedometer checks was not located in the documented searches. Official Oregon Department of Transportation driver education supplies that perceptual advice; no foreign laws or limits are imported. [Evidence and search log](evidence.md).

Validation passed: 47 manuscript blocks, source links, internal navigation, fonts/text bounds, 76 official sign placements, 13 approved scenes, separated answers and reproducible build. All 50 rendered pages inspected, with full-size checks on 11, 13, 25, 27, 48, 49 and 50. [Validation](validation.json).

The question bank, both 498-page review PDFs, all 154 G0 snapshots and other chapter PDFs remain unchanged. Other modules, M06-L02/L04 and review text are unchanged. G1–G6 now teach **24 of 55 gaps**; **31 remain** for G7–G10. Final assembly/pages and whole-bank coverage audit await G11/G12. G7 has not been executed.

questions.question_prompt: After a long motorway drive, 60 km/h feels unusually slow. What should you do?
questions.keyed_answer: Check the speedometer and adapt to the new road conditions.
questions.teaching_excerpt: After a long period at a steady motorway speed, your perception can adapt to that pace. On a slower road, the correct lower speed may feel unusually slow. This effect is often called speed adaptation or velocitation. Check the speedometer regularly to judge actual speed and adjust to the current limit and conditions. The feeling alone is not evidence that the speedometer is faulty. ODOT: speed perception and speedometer checks Worked transition. After a long motorway trip, you leave onto a road signed 50 km/h. At 50, the car feels as if it is crawling. Confirm the speedometer reading, read the new road and retain a speed suited to its limit, visibility and hazards. Do not accelerate merely to recover the motorway's familiar feeling.
questions.coverage_reasoning: Explains steady-speed perceptual adaptation, deceptive slow feeling, speedometer checks, current limit/conditions and motorway-to-50 example. Feeling alone does not establish instrument fault.

questions.question_prompt: Heavy traffic makes a country-road left turn unsafe. What is a sensible alternative?
questions.keyed_answer: Continue to a suitable turning place and return for a right turn.
questions.teaching_excerpt: On an ordinary two-way rural road, heavy traffic may make a direct left turn unsafe. Continue to a suitable, permitted place or route where you can change direction safely, then return to approach the destination with a right turn if that movement is allowed and safe. This can avoid hazardous waiting and crossing the opposing stream at the original entrance. It is a planning alternative, not permission to turn around immediately on the carriageway. If no safe legal return route exists, choose another route or postpone. Trafikverket: example of routing to a turning place Legal boundary. Before turning or leaving the road, protect oncoming traffic and traffic on the road you enter; take particular care of following traffic. A turnaround must cause neither danger nor obstruction. Signs and access restrictions still apply. Never turn around or reverse on a motorway or expressway. If you can wait safely and legally for a left turn, remember the advice in M04-L02 to keep the front wheels straight; that advice does not make an unsafe turn suitable. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§24, 26, 29 and 46; chapter 9 §§1–2 Worked rural alternative. A farm entrance is on your left and busy traffic leaves no safe opportunity. You continue to an accessible junction route that legally and safely brings you back in the opposite direction. The entrance is then on your right. Check people, traffic and the entrance again before turning; the revised route does not guarantee a safe final movement. Wil

questions.question_prompt: When is extra attention to large animals especially important?
questions.keyed_answer: Around dusk and dawn near wildlife habitats and fence openings.
questions.teaching_excerpt: Give extra attention at dawn and dusk, near animal habitats and where fences end or have openings. Scan woodland edges, bushes and small waterways beside the road: Trafikverket's road-project study describes these as animal routes that can conceal an approach. Its national guidance also describes animal passages through fence openings. These are cues for observation and speed planning, not predictions that animals only cross there. Trafikverket: wildlife and fence passages · Trafikverket: habitat example, page 9 Apply the cues. At dusk, woodland meets a field beside a gap in the fence. Read the edges and opening as possible animal approaches, and choose speed for the view and foreseeable hazard. Keep observing even on fenced stretches. Prevention belongs here; actions after a collision are in M10-L01.

# G6 evidence

Checked 13 October 2026. Three essential claims. Rural return-right routing is a conditional editorial inference, not a verbatim general agency recommendation.

## Complex Driving Skills — Online Parent Guide to Teen Driving

Oregon Department of Transportation, Driver and Motor Vehicle Services. Live official guide; publication/update date not displayed in inspected passage. [Source](https://www.oregon.gov/odot/dmv/pages/online_parent_guide_to_teen_driving/08_complex_driving_skills.aspx).

Locator: Highway glossary: Velocitation; Exiting the Freeway, steps 5–6. Short excerpt: “Make sure you do frequent speedometer checks to help adjust your speed.”.

Support: Prolonged steady-speed driving can alter perceived speed; speedometer checks help adjustment after leaving fast traffic.

Scope: Perceptual/safety advice only. No foreign traffic laws, speed limits or stopping distances imported; feeling slow does not prove instrument failure, nor establish an instrument can never fail.

Fallback: Targeted TS/TRV searches did not locate exact speed-adaptation and instrument-check guidance. VTI results inspected did not establish this complete transition advice. ODOT provides direct official driver education.

## Avstängning för förberedande arbeten — E4 Förbifart Stockholm
